extracted.intended_audience: States developing section 111 state plans, power-sector regulated entities, grid operators, Tribal nations, and other stakeholders participating in the EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria EPA used in the final rule preamble for evaluating environmental justice, benefits, outreach, and grid reliability implications of the section 111 power-sector rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA definition of Environmental Justice (EJ)
rubrics_metrics.description: EJ is “the just treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of income, race, color, national origin, Tribal affiliation, or disability, in agency decision-making and other Federal activities that affect human health and the environment so that people: (i) Are fully protected from disproportionate and adverse human health and environmental effects (including risks) and hazards, including those related to climate change, the cumulative impacts of environmental and other burdens, and the legacy of racism or other structural or systemic barriers; and (ii) have equitable access to a healthy, sustainable, and resilient environment in which to live, play, work, learn, grow, worship, and engage in cultural and subsistence practices.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this two-part definition as the framing for EJ analyses: (i) protecting communities from disproportionate harms (including cumulative and climate-related harms and structural barriers) and (ii) ensuring equitable access to healthy environments. Interpret analyses through both protection-from-harm and equitable-access lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: EJ triggers under EPA Technical Guidance (June 2016)
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulatory action may involve potential EJ concerns if it could: (1) Create new disproportionate impacts on communities with EJ concerns; (2) Exacerbate existing disproportionate impacts on communities with EJ concerns; or (3) Present opportunities to address existing disproportionate impacts on communities with EJ concerns through this action under development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When screening for EJ issues, evaluate whether the proposed regulatory action meets any of the three triggers. Document evidence and uncertainty for each trigger rather than relying on assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three EJ analysis questions (from EJ technical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of potential EJ concerns for regulatory actions should address three questions: (1) Are there potential EJ concerns associated with environmental stressors affected by the regulatory action for population groups of concern in the baseline? (2) Are there potential EJ concerns associated with environmental stressors affected by the regulatory action for population groups of concern for the regulatory option(s) under consideration? (3) For the regulatory option(s) under consideration, are potential EJ concerns created or mitigated compared to the baseline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the EJ section to explicitly answer these three questions. Separately present baseline conditions, projected post-policy outcomes, and comparative (post vs baseline) analyses, and be explicit about uncertainties and limitations for each question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of two complementary analyses for EJ: proximity and exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA employs two types of analysis to respond to the EJ questions: proximity analyses and exposure analyses. Both can inform whether there are potential EJ concerns for population groups of concern in the baseline (question 1), while exposure analyses (based on future air quality modeling) inform whether regulatory options create or mitigate EJ concerns (questions 2 and 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct both analyses because they answer different questions; do not directly compare them as equivalent. Clearly state which EJ question each analysis is intended to address and report limitations unique to each approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity analysis of populations near affected facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline demographic proximity analyses identify populations that may be exposed to local environmental stressors by evaluating demographics living within specified distances (e.g., within 5 km, 10 km, 50 km) of affected facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proximity metrics to screen for communities potentially at risk (e.g., higher percentages of American Indian, below-poverty populations). Explicitly note that proximity does not capture variation in baseline exposures and does not prove exposures or impacts will occur; present full methodology (distance bands, facility lists) and link to technical reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure analysis using air quality modeling with defined metrics and resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure analyses are based on future air quality modeling under illustrative compliance scenarios and use pollutant metrics consistent with the benefits assessment: for ozone, the maximum daily 8-hour average averaged across the April–September warm season (AS‑MO3); for PM2.5, the annual average. Modeling used state and fuel level emission data paired with facility-level baseline emissions at a resolution of 12 square kilometers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing exposure analyses, specify pollutant metrics, model resolution, scenario assumptions, and the link between emissions and concentration changes. Acknowledge that chosen metrics may smooth gradients (e.g., AS‑MO3 smooths daily ozone peaks and is not directly relatable to NAAQS) and that model resolution and scenario choice influence detectability of localized impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and uncertainty statements for exposure analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure analyses are subject to caveats: they are based on illustrative state compliance scenarios and do not consider the potential impact of meaningful engagement or other protections; they are relative to modeled baselines which have projection uncertainty (especially in later years); pollutant metrics are limited to those used in the benefits assessment; model resolution limits granularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list caveats and quantify uncertainty where possible. Avoid over‑interpreting small modeled concentration changes relative to baseline levels; discuss the potential for unassessed localized impacts and data limitations (e.g., neighborhood-scale disparities, redlined areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present exposure results in aggregated and distributional formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure analysis results should be provided in two formats: aggregated (national- and state-level overviews) and distributional (detailed information about concentration changes experienced by everyone within each population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both views: aggregated results for policy-level summaries and distributional results to show variation across and within demographic groups. Use distributional outputs to detect small, localized disproportionate impacts that aggregated results may mask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation principle: compare exposure changes to baseline disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: Because modeled post-policy ozone and PM2.5 changes are small relative to baseline concentrations and disparities, analyses should assess whether post-policy burdens remain and whether changes materially alter disparities (i.e., whether EJ concerns are created, exacerbated, or mitigated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus interpretation on magnitude relative to baseline disparities, not only statistical change. Explicitly report when changes are too small to alter existing disparities and identify any demographic groups or years where slight exacerbation or mitigation may occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline exposure disparity identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline ozone and PM2.5 exposure analyses should identify demographic groups with higher exposures (examples identified here include residents of redlined tracts, linguistically isolated populations, Hispanic and Asian populations, persons without high school diplomas, American Indian and Tribal lands residents, children, unemployed populations, and Black populations for PM2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report which groups exhibit higher baseline exposures, quantify disparities, and note where additional analyses are needed to understand implications. Do not assume baseline equality across groups even if absolute levels are relatively low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for meaningful engagement by states in state-plan development
rubrics_metrics.description: States are required, as part of the state plan development process, to conduct meaningful engagement with stakeholders. The EPA finalized revisions requiring meaningful engagement (see subpart Ba implementing regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and document outreach activities (e.g., pre-proposal dockets, webinars targeted to Tribal and EJ communities, public hearings). Describe how meaningful engagement informed state planning and how it could mitigate localized emissions increases. Include timelines and opportunities for input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong encouragement for states to consult reliability authorities and share unit-specific information
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of meaningful engagement, states are strongly encouraged to consult relevant balancing authorities and reliability coordinators for affected sources and to share available unit-specific requirements and compliance information in a timely fashion to promote early and informed reliability planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should document consultation with balancing authorities, transmission planners, and reliability coordinators and provide unit-specific compliance timelines and data to facilitate coordinated regional planning and avoid cross-jurisdictional reliability impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rules and flexibilities to avoid impairing grid reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules include flexibilities and adjustments to accommodate planning decisions and ensure reliable operation of the bulk-power system, including restructuring subcategories (e.g., not finalizing imminent/near-term subcategory), excluding units with cease dates before Jan 1, 2032, extending CCS compliance timelines by 2 years for long‑term subcategory, and not finalizing certain proposed standards (e.g., 30% hydrogen co‑firing BSER for some turbines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing standards, consider timing, subcategory scope, and technology lead times. Use regulatory adjustments to provide planning latitude, avoid regulating units that will retire imminently, and allow more time where infrastructure constraints exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible state compliance flexibilities (RULOF, averaging, trading, mass-based compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: States may use a suite of voluntary compliance flexibilities to address reliability concerns: RULOF to establish source-specific standards and compliance schedules, emission averaging and trading, unit-specific mass-based compliance mechanisms for certain subcategories—provided they achieve an equivalent level of emission reduction consistent with individual rate-based standards of performance, and for certain mechanisms include a backstop emission rate, and offering compliance date extensions for unanticipated control-technology implementation delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If states adopt averaging/trading or unit-specific mass-based approaches, they must demonstrate equivalence with rate-based standards and include safeguards (e.g., backstop emission rate). Document RULOF justifications and ensure compliance schedules are feasible and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term reliability mechanism for acute system emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A short-term reliability mechanism is available for new and existing units and is designed to provide additional flexibility through an alternative compliance strategy during acute system emergencies that threaten reliability. States may elect to include this mechanism in their plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define emergency criteria, eligibility, and procedural steps for invoking the mechanism. If states include the mechanism, ensure the mechanism's scope, duration, and monitoring are clearly specified so it can be presumptively approvable if it meets the emission-guideline requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability assurance mechanism for temporarily retained units
rubrics_metrics.description: A reliability assurance mechanism is available for existing units that intend to cease operating but, for unforeseen reasons, need to temporarily remain online to support reliability beyond the planned cease operation date. It requires a specific and adequate showing of reliability need satisfactory to EPA, is intended where there is insufficient time to complete a state plan revision, and is limited to the amount of time substantiated (may not exceed 1 year). EPA intends to consult with FERC for needs exceeding 6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications should include concrete evidence of reliability need, substantiated duration, and supporting consultation with reliability authorities. Expect EPA review and possible consultation with FERC for longer durations. Time limits and evidentiary burden are strict; design plans to avoid routine reliance on this mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptive approvability condition for state-incorporated reliability instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: These short-term and reliability assurance instruments will be presumptively approvable, provided they meet the requirements defined in the emission guidelines, if states choose to incorporate them into their plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When states draft plan provisions for these mechanisms, ensure they align explicitly with the emission-guideline requirements (eligibility, evidence standards, duration limits, monitoring) to streamline EPA approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and use of DOE section 202(c) emergency authority
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE has authority under section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to order temporary generation in certain emergency conditions; an affected source operating pursuant to such an order is deemed not to be operating in violation of its environmental requirements. Orders may be issued for 90 days and extended in 90-day increments after consultation with EPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with DOE and understand section 202(c) as an available federal emergency backstop. Document interactions and any 202(c) requests/orders in state plans or compliance narratives when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource adequacy and sensitivity analyses to evaluate reliability impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA performed capacity expansion modeling and a variety of sensitivity analyses (including higher electricity demand scenarios and interactions with other pending power-sector rules) and examined technical memoranda (IPM Sensitivity Runs; Resource Adequacy Analysis) to evaluate resource adequacy and confirm available compliance pathways that respect NERC reliability considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analyses should include capacity expansion modeling and targeted sensitivity runs (e.g., higher demand, different retirement assumptions) and document whether identified compliance pathways meet reliability constraints. Share underlying technical memos and model assumptions in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: External peer review and response for SC-GHG and modeling updates
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA initiated an external peer review of the technical report for SC-GHG estimates; peer reviewers commended the draft update and recommended refinements (presentation, future modeling improvements, especially climate change impacts and associated damages not currently included). EPA incorporated discussion of omitted impacts and other updates to address recommendations, and made peer review materials available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For major methodological updates (e.g., social cost estimates), conduct external peer review, transparently respond to each recommendation, and incorporate or document why recommendations were not adopted. Make peer reviewer selection, reports, and agency responses publicly available.
